title: Make Your Mark
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Wootton opens with a memory of his father's high school English classroom, where the bulletin board was layered with whatever the students chose to hang: cartoons, comic book characters, poems. It was a mess, but it was theirs, and it stood against the immaculate teacher-designed boards of his own elementary school. From that he builds an argument about who owns a classroom, quoting retired educator Wanda Lincoln on what a perfect room communicates at the start of the year and Tom Rademacher on a classroom as something teacher and students build together. The bulk of the piece is a workshop he designed with visual artist Tommaso Iskra De Silvestri for sixth graders in the Everett Public Schools, aimed at the question of how students might visually transform their own classroom. Students analyzed the Black Panther's mask and Lucha Libre masks for the characteristics they signal, then worked under the guiding question of how masks both hide and reveal us. To push past derivative superhero imagery, Wootton borrowed kennings from Old English and Norse poetry, having students build word banks and combine nouns and verbs into compound self-descriptions like Reading Wolf and Breathing Books, which quietly taught suffixes and word transformation without a grammar lesson. Masks were cut Matisse style from folded paper, then each student chose where in the room to exhibit the work, including the lockers a teacher had previously labeled with owls in her own handwriting.
points: The lockers are the pivotal example: student-chosen images replacing owls labeled in the teacher's handwriting, with student art beginning to displace inspirational posters.
Kennings function as a pedagogical workaround, moving students to a poetic and symbolic register so their masks would not simply copy current superheroes.
Building kennings required manipulating suffixes to turn verbs into adjectives and nouns, which Wootton notes happened without any formal grammar lesson.
The mask analysis starts from texts students already know, reading the Black Panther costume and a Lucha Libre wrestler's wings as deliberate signals of character.
Wootton frames blank institutional walls as an opportunity rather than a deficit, and closes on Whitman's line about contributing a verse as the message a transformed space sends.
quotes: My father’s bulletin board was different. He let the students bring in practically anything they wanted and hang it—there were layers upon layers of cartoons, comic book characters, and poems. It was a mess, but it was theirs.

Wanda Lincoln, a retired educator, in a speech to elementary school teachers said, “When we as teachers make sure the room is perfect at the beginning of the school year, we are sending the message that the classroom is ours, not the students.
I’ve just never wanted my classroom to feel like my space. A classroom, in so many ways, is something that a teacher and students build together.

We knew if we simply asked the students to create a “superhero” masks we would get many masks derivative of today’s heroes. We needed to find a way to move students to a more poetic and symbolic way of imagining their masks.
a compound expression in Old English and Old Norse poetry with metaphorical meaning, e.g., oar-steed = ship.
Without any formal grammar lesson, students naturally began manipulating, transforming, and combining words.

The image above of the lockers is the best example of how we might rethink our classroom spaces. Before, the teacher put an owl on each students’ locker and in the teacher’s handwriting wrote their name.

Schools are big. Blank walls are everywhere. We can teach in institutional spaces, or, with the help of our students, transform them into beautiful, magical places to learn. In doing so, we show students that these spaces belong to all of us and that they too can “contribute a verse.
